passages.title: Lichen survey
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Many lichens are sensitive to sulfur dioxide, an air pollutant.
- In a 2015 survey, volunteers counted lichen species on trees across a city.
- Sites far from major roads had an average of 11 lichen species; sites near major roads had an average of 4.
- The survey did not measure sulfur dioxide directly.
- Lichens can also be affected by tree bark acidity and by shade.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: An inevitable treaty?
passages.text: Although the historian's account of the treaty negotiations is meticulously documented, her conclusion that the agreement was inevitable seems ______, since several of the letters she herself cites show delegates on the verge of abandoning the talks.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Spines on demand
passages.text: Some water fleas grow protective spines only when they detect chemicals released by their predator, a midge larva. The spines lower a flea's risk of being eaten but slow its reproduction. Researchers collected fleas from a lake where midge larvae had been absent for several decades and exposed them to midge chemicals in the laboratory. These fleas grew spines just as readily as fleas taken from lakes where midges were common, which suggests that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Shade trees
passages.text:
A city planted trees along some streets in 2019 to reduce summer heat. A researcher compared average midday street-surface temperatures in July.
Streets with new trees: 41°C in 2018; 38°C in 2023.
Streets without new trees: 40°C in 2018; 40°C in 2023.
The researcher concludes that the trees, rather than a citywide change in weather, most likely explain the cooling on the planted streets.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Dating a map
passages.text: The museum's oldest map was long thought to date from the early ______ recent analysis of its paper, however, suggests that it was drawn more than a century later.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Saturn's rings
passages.text: For two centuries after their discovery, many astronomers assumed that Saturn's rings were solid sheets of material. In the 1850s, the physicist James Clerk Maxwell showed mathematically that a solid ring of that size would be torn apart by Saturn's gravity. ______ he argued, the rings must consist of countless separate particles, each orbiting the planet on its own.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Tree rings and a shipwreck
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Divers found the wreck of a wooden ship in the Baltic Sea.
- Radiocarbon dating of the wood gave a possible range of about 150 years.
- Each year's weather affects how wide a tree's growth ring is, so a sequence of rings forms a pattern unique to those years.
- Researchers matched the ring pattern in the ship's oak planks to a regional record of tree-ring widths.
- The match showed that the trees were cut down in the winter of 1611-1612.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A mixed review
passages.text: The critic's praise for the new film was ______: although she admired its cinematography, she devoted most of her review to faulting the script, the pacing, and the lead performance.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Marigolds and nematodes
passages.text: Farmers have long noticed that tomato plants grown beside marigolds suffer less damage from root-knot nematodes, tiny worms that attack roots. One explanation is that marigold roots release a compound that is toxic to the nematodes; another is that marigolds encourage the growth of soil fungi that prey on nematodes. To test these ideas, researchers sterilized a batch of soil, killing any fungi, and then added equal numbers of nematodes to sterilized and unsterilized pots, each containing a tomato plant beside a marigold. Nematode numbers ended up just as low in the sterilized pots as in the unsterilized ones, and both were far lower than in comparison pots without marigolds, which suggests that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A reading app
passages.text:
A school district gave a reading app to some students in grades 4 and 5 and compared their gains on a spring reading test with the gains of students who did not use the app.
Students who began the year below grade level: app users gained 14 points; nonusers gained 6 points.
Students who began the year at grade level: app users gained 9 points; nonusers gained 5 points.
A district analyst concludes that the app benefited students who began below grade level more than it benefited students who began at grade level.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Why a dialect fades
passages.text:
Text 1
In the valleys of one mountain region, younger residents use far fewer of the region's traditional dialect features than their grandparents do. A linguist attributes the change to television, arguing that decades of exposure to broadcast speech have pulled local speakers toward a national standard.

Text 2
Sociolinguist Mara Vint interviewed residents of the same region who reported watching similar amounts of television. Those who had spent several years working in distant cities had dropped most dialect features, while those who had always lived in the valleys still used them heavily. Vint argues that face-to-face contact with speakers of other varieties, not broadcast speech, reshapes how people talk.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The order slip
passages.text: Mrs. Avery had kept the bookshop for thirty years and prided herself on finding any book a customer could name. When a young man came in asking for a novel she had never heard of, she smiled and promised to order it. After he left, she wrote the title on a slip of paper, studied it for a long moment, and then tucked it into the drawer where she kept the letters she did not intend to answer.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Newton's telescope
passages.text: Early telescopes surrounded their images with fringes of false color, because their glass lenses bent different colors of light by different amounts. Isaac Newton concluded, wrongly as it turned out, that no arrangement of lenses could ever remove this flaw. ______ he built a telescope that gathered light with a curved mirror, which reflects all colors equally.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A careful report
passages.text: The review committee's report on the proposed stadium was notably ______: it listed the plan's costs and benefits in detail but declined to say whether the city should go ahead with the project.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Roman harbor concrete
passages.text: Some concrete structures built in Roman harbors have survived roughly two thousand years of exposure to seawater, while modern concrete in similar conditions can crumble within decades. The difference long puzzled engineers. Analyzing samples from Roman harbors, researchers found that seawater seeping through the concrete reacted with volcanic ash in the original mix, growing new mineral crystals that filled cracks and strengthened the material over time.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Crows and masks
passages.text: In a long-term study, researchers wearing a distinctive mask briefly captured and released several wild crows on a college campus. For years afterward, crows on the campus scolded and dived at anyone wearing that mask but ignored people wearing a different, neutral mask. The researchers hypothesized that crows learn to recognize dangerous people not only from their own experience but also by observing other crows.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Birds along trails
passages.text: An ecologist surveyed bird species in a forest by having observers walk the forest's trails at dawn and record every species they heard singing. Observers recorded more species near trailheads than deep in the forest. However, because the observers walked only along trails and could hear birds only within about fifty meters, the ecologist cautioned that ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A shorter week
passages.text:
Text 1
An economist studying companies that adopted a four-day workweek found that their output per employee rose by an average of 8 percent in the following year. She argues that a shorter week could raise productivity across the economy.

Text 2
A labor researcher notes that the companies in the study chose to try the four-day week, and many were firms whose managers already believed their work could be done in less time. Results from such firms, he argues, may say little about how a shorter week would work at companies that would not have chosen it.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Two writers
passages.text: Having spent a decade comparing the handwriting, ink, and paper of the letters, ______ that they were written by two different people rather than one.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Load ratings
passages.text: The new bridge across the river was designed to carry far heavier traffic than the one it replaced. ______ engineers rated it to support trucks weighing up to forty tons, about twice the limit on the old bridge.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Early results
passages.text: Although the new treatment's early results were promising, the researchers were careful not to ______ them, noting that the trial had included only forty patients and had lasted just six weeks.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: The ferry
passages.text: The old ferry had crossed the river twice a day for sixty years. Most people in town no longer noticed its horn. When the county announced that a new bridge would replace it, people who had not ridden the ferry in decades wrote letters to the newspaper demanding that it be saved.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Desert seeds
passages.text: The seeds of a certain desert plant contain a chemical that prevents them from germinating. Heavy rainfall washes the chemical out of the seed coat, but a light shower does not. In laboratory tests, seeds soaked in water for a few minutes rarely germinated, while seeds soaked for several hours germinated readily. This mechanism likely benefits the plant because ______
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Two cities
passages.text:
A demographer compared the populations of two cities.
City A: 50,000 residents in 2000; 80,000 residents in 2020.
City B: 120,000 residents in 2000; 150,000 residents in 2020.
The demographer claims that although the two cities gained the same number of residents, city A grew much faster in percentage terms.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A popular gallery
passages.text: The museum's newest gallery, which opened in ______ already drawn more visitors than any other exhibit in the building's history.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: A summer tradition
passages.text: The tradition of building sandcastles on the town's beach each July, which began more than a century ago as a contest for local children, ______ to draw thousands of visitors every summer.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: An unexplored cave
passages.text: Early accounts described the cave as a single, modest chamber. Later surveys found it to be far larger, with dozens of connected passages stretching for kilometers. ______ the original explorers, working by candlelight, had seen only the entrance hall.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Axolotl regrowth
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The axolotl is a salamander native to lakes near Mexico City.
- Unlike most salamanders, it keeps its gills and lives in water as an adult.
- It can regrow lost limbs, including bone and muscle.
- Researchers have found that axolotls regrow limbs more slowly as they age.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Rural and urban survey
passages.text: In a state survey, 200 rural residents and 800 urban residents were asked whether they had used a public library in the past month. Of the rural residents, 30 percent said yes; of the urban residents, 20 percent said yes. A reporter claims that more urban residents than rural residents in the survey had used a library, even though a smaller percentage of urban residents had.
passages.author: ai:claude

passages.title: Two great rivers
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The Amazon River carries more water to the sea than any other river.
- The Congo River carries the second-largest volume of water.
- Both rivers drain large tropical rainforests.
- The Amazon is roughly 6,400 kilometers long; the Congo is roughly 4,700 kilometers long.
- Parts of the Congo are more than 200 meters deep.
passages.author: ai:claude

questions.evidence: ferns crowded every bench, and vines had climbed all the way to the cracked glass roof
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

choices.A: teeming
choices.B: devoid
choices.C: reminiscent
choices.D: wary

questions.explanation: The colon introduces evidence that the greenhouse was full of plants. "Teeming with life" means crowded with living things, which matches ferns on every bench and vines up to the roof.

distractor_explanations.B: "Devoid" means completely lacking, the opposite of what the details describe.
distractor_explanations.C: "Reminiscent" means suggestive of something else and is followed by "of," not "with"; it does not describe abundance.
distractor_explanations.D: "Wary" means cautious, a quality of people or animals, not of a greenhouse.

hints: What do the details after the colon show about the greenhouse?
Predict a word meaning 'full of' before reading the choices.

strategy.explanation: Predict "full," then choose the closest precise word.

questions.remember: Let the text's evidence choose the word.

questions.evidence: "A long span on a weak foundation," he says, "is simply a dramatic way to fail."
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the quotation in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It presents a counterargument that Reyes goes on to reject.
choices.B: It explains how engineers measure the span of a bridge.
choices.C: It illustrates, in memorable terms, why Reyes believes a bridge's foundation matters more than its span.
choices.D: It suggests that most existing bridges were built on weak foundations.

questions.explanation: Reyes claims the foundation is the most important part of a bridge. The quotation backs that claim with a vivid image: however impressive the span, a weak foundation means failure.

distractor_explanations.A: The quotation is Reyes's own statement supporting his view, not a counterargument.
distractor_explanations.B: The quotation says nothing about how spans are measured.
distractor_explanations.D: The quotation describes a hypothetical case and makes no claim about most existing bridges.

hints: What is Reyes's main claim?
How does the quotation relate to that claim?

strategy.explanation: Identify the claim first, then ask how the quotation serves it.

questions.remember: Function questions ask what a part does for the whole.

choices.C: Volunteers in Alder Creek are paid to repair residents' household items.
choices.D: Residents of Alder Creek throw away fewer items than residents of other towns do.

distractor_explanations.D: The text makes no comparison with other towns.

questions.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the student's conclusion?

choices.A: Feeder 1, which held sunflower seeds, had 212 visits, more than either the thistle feeder (87) or the suet feeder (145).
choices.B: Feeder 2, which held thistle seeds, had 87 visits, fewer than Feeder 3.
choices.C: Together, the three feeders received 444 visits.
choices.D: Feeder 3, which held suet, had 145 visits.

questions.explanation: The conclusion is that sunflower seeds attracted the most visits. Supporting it requires comparing the sunflower feeder with both others: 212 is greater than 87 and 145. Only A makes that full comparison.

distractor_explanations.B: This compares only the other two feeders and says nothing about sunflower seeds.
distractor_explanations.C: The total does not show which food attracted the most visits.
distractor_explanations.D: One feeder's count alone cannot show which food was most popular.

hints: What exactly does the conclusion claim?
Which choice compares sunflower seeds with both other foods?

strategy.explanation: Restate the claim, then choose the data that compares all three.

distractor_explanations.C: With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.
distractor_explanations.D: "Which" makes the second part a relative clause, but the rest of the sentence ("within ten years, the number … had tripled") cannot follow "which" grammatically.

questions.evidence: Glass can be recycled again and again without losing quality.
questions.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between recycling glass and recycling plastic. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Glass bottles and plastic bottles can both be recycled.
choices.B: Recycled glass is often used to make new bottles.
choices.C: Both glass and plastic are commonly used to make bottles, and both can be recycled.
choices.D: Glass can be recycled again and again without losing quality, whereas most plastics can be recycled only a few times before the material degrades.

questions.explanation: The goal is a difference. D contrasts how many times each material can be recycled, using "whereas" to make the difference explicit.

distractor_explanations.A: This states a similarity, not a difference.
distractor_explanations.B: This gives information about glass only, with no comparison to plastic.
distractor_explanations.C: This states similarities between the materials.

hints: The goal is to emphasize a difference.
Which choice mentions both materials and contrasts them?

strategy.explanation: Underline the goal (difference), then eliminate choices that state similarities or mention one material.

questions.remember: Synthesis questions: the stated goal decides the answer.

questions.evidence: Yet when researchers measured trehalose in several tardigrade species, they found little or none.
questions.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It presents two competing explanations and concludes that neither is supported.
choices.B: It describes an experiment and then lists that experiment's limitations.
choices.C: It describes a long-held assumption, presents evidence against it, and then reports an alternative explanation.
choices.D: It introduces an animal and compares it with other organisms that produce trehalose.

questions.explanation: The text opens with an assumption (trehalose protects tardigrades), gives evidence against it (little or no trehalose found), and ends with an alternative (tardigrade-specific proteins forming a gel).

distractor_explanations.A: The text does reach a supported explanation: the proteins.
distractor_explanations.B: No limitations of an experiment are listed.
distractor_explanations.D: The text mentions other organisms only briefly and does not compare tardigrades with them.

hints: Track the text sentence by sentence: assumption, then what?
What does the last sentence offer?

strategy.explanation: Label each sentence's role, then match the sequence.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: scientist's
choices.B: scientists
choices.C: scientists's
choices.D: scientists'

questions.explanation: The findings belong to two scientists, so the plural possessive is needed. For a plural noun ending in s, add only an apostrophe: "scientists'."

distractor_explanations.B: "Scientists" without an apostrophe is a plain plural, not a possessive.
distractor_explanations.C: "Scientists's" is not standard for a plural possessive.

hints: How many scientists are there?
How is a plural noun ending in s made possessive?

strategy.explanation: Plural + possessive = s'.

questions.remember: Plural possessive: add just an apostrophe after s.

questions.evidence: Some critics predicted that the redesigned riverside park would attract few visitors.
questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Similarly,
choices.B: Therefore,
choices.C: On the contrary,
choices.D: For example,

questions.explanation: The critics predicted few visitors; attendance instead doubled. "On the contrary" signals that the second sentence contradicts the prediction.

distractor_explanations.B: Without a comma after "March," the clause "which opened in March" is opened by a comma but never closed.
distractor_explanations.C: A semicolon cannot separate the subject "gallery" from its verb "has drawn."
distractor_explanations.D: A dash cannot close a clause that was opened with a comma; the punctuation must match.

hints: Where does the interrupting clause begin and end?

strategy.explanation: Match the closing punctuation to the opening comma.

questions.remember: A nonessential clause in mid-sentence needs matching punctuation on both sides.

questions.remember: A verb agrees with its subject, not with the nearest noun.

questions.subskill: Rhetorical synthesis (presenting a finding to a new audience)
questions.evidence: Researchers have found that axolotls regrow limbs more slowly as they age.
questions.stem: The student wants to present the research finding to an audience unfamiliar with axolotls. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Researchers have found that axolotls regrow lost limbs, including bone and muscle, more slowly with age.
choices.B: The axolotl, a salamander from lakes near Mexico City, keeps its gills and lives in water as an adult.
choices.C: Axolotls, salamanders from near Mexico City that can regrow lost limbs, regrow them more slowly with age.
choices.D: Unlike most salamanders, axolotls keep their gills as adults and can even regrow their lost limbs.

questions.explanation: Only C both introduces the axolotl (a salamander from near Mexico City that regrows limbs) and states the finding.

distractor_explanations.A: This presents the finding but never explains what an axolotl is for an unfamiliar audience.
distractor_explanations.B: This introduces the animal but omits the research finding.
distractor_explanations.D: This describes the animal's traits but leaves out the finding about age.

hints: What does an unfamiliar audience need besides the finding?

strategy.explanation: Check for an introduction and the finding.

questions.remember: For a new audience, introduce the subject as you present the point.

questions.evidence: more urban residents than rural residents in the survey had used a library
questions.stem: Which choice best uses data from the survey to support the reporter's claim?

choices.A: 160 urban residents said yes versus 60 rural residents, though 20 percent is below 30 percent.
choices.B: 60 rural residents said yes, which is 30 percent of the 200 rural residents who were surveyed.
choices.C: 160 urban residents said yes, which is 20 percent of the 800 urban residents who were surveyed.
choices.D: Of the 1,000 residents surveyed, 220 said yes, and 800 of the 1,000 lived in urban areas.

questions.explanation: 20 percent of 800 is 160 and 30 percent of 200 is 60, so more urban residents said yes even though their percentage was lower. Only A gives both parts.

distractor_explanations.B: This gives only the rural count and percentage, so it cannot show that more urban residents said yes.
distractor_explanations.C: This gives only the urban count and percentage, so it cannot show that more urban than rural residents said yes.
distractor_explanations.D: A combined total does not show how the yes answers split between urban and rural residents.

hints: What would you need to compute to compare numbers of people?

strategy.explanation: Convert each percentage to a count.

questions.remember: A smaller percentage of a larger group can still be a larger number.

questions.evidence: Both rivers drain large tropical rainforests.
questions.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the two rivers. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: At roughly 6,400 kilometers, the Amazon is about 1,700 kilometers longer than the 4,700-kilometer Congo.
choices.B: Parts of the Congo River are more than 200 meters deep, making it unusually deep for a river.
choices.C: The Amazon River carries more water to the sea than any other river anywhere on Earth, including the Congo.
choices.D: The Amazon and Congo both drain large tropical rainforests and rank first and second in water volume.

questions.explanation: Only D describes features the two rivers share: both drain rainforests and both are at the top in volume.

distractor_explanations.A: This emphasizes a difference in length, not a similarity.
distractor_explanations.B: This describes only the Congo.
distractor_explanations.C: This describes only the Amazon.

hints: Which choice mentions both rivers and something they have in common?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against the goal.

questions.remember: For a similarity goal, the answer must describe both items and what they share.
